cf.title: pg_upgrade fails when FK constraint with same name exists on partitioned table and its partition

input.subject: pg_upgrade fails when FK constraint with same name exists on partitioned table and its partition

verdict_reasoning: The failure is real and reproducible, but the design is not settled. The check also fails for clusters that would upgrade fine (standards-compat-1), and the thread has not weighed a warning, a narrow query, or a pg_dump ordering fix (maintenance-fit-2). Demand rests on one report, and the one committer in the thread doubted the check is worth adding (demand-1). The release scope is also open (standards-compat-2).

brief.title: pg_upgrade --check for same-named NOT VALID FKs on partition and parent
brief.problem: pg_upgrade from Postgres 11 through 17 can fail in pg_restore when a partition has its own NOT VALID foreign key with the same name as an FK on its parent. pg_upgrade --check reports "Clusters are compatible" and the real run then fails with "constraint ... for relation ... already exists". This affects users who upgrade clusters with such partitions.
brief.proposed_design: pg_upgrade --check gets a new check that queries the old cluster for NOT VALID FKs on partitions that share a name with an FK on the parent and have conparentid = 0. The check runs only for old clusters from version 11 through 17. pg_dump output is unchanged. v2 adds quoted, schema-qualified names in the report, "may fail" wording, a hint that prefers rename, and a TAP test.
user_visible_surface: New pg_upgrade --check failure that lists affected partition FKs as schema.table.constraint, quoted in v2.
New hint text: rename the partition's constraint, or drop it when it matches the parent's FK (v2 wording).
New TAP test src/bin/pg_upgrade/t/010_duplicate_fk_names.pl, which runs only when oldinstall points to a version 11-17 install.
author_claims: Only NOT VALID FKs are affected, because before commit b663b9436e7 ATTACH PARTITION did not link them to the parent's FK.
CHECK, PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, EXCLUDE and NOT NULL constraints cannot cause this conflict.
Whether the restore fails depends on pg_dump's sort order, and the check flags both orders on purpose.
The reviewer reports that v1 catches all 5 failing cases out of 13 tested, and also flags 5 cases that would have upgraded fine.
The reviewer argues a narrow query would copy pg_dump's internal sort order and could silently miss cases if that order changes.
brief.thread_state: Álvaro Herrera doubted a --check was worth adding and declined to change pg_dump or pg_upgrade restore behaviour. João Rito reviewed v1, posted v2-0002 (report and hint) and v2-0003 (test), but neither the author nor a committer has replied to v2.
unclear: Whether Álvaro or another committer accepts the broad check with its false positives, which block upgrades that would succeed.
The thread has no test against old versions 11 through 16, with meson, or on Windows.
Whether the author agrees with the v2-0002 changes to the report and hint.
Whether a check this specific should also be back-patched; the thread names only master.

prior_attempts.title: pg_upgrade fails with non-standard ACL
prior_attempts.quote: I'm not generally enthusiastic about adding pg_upgrade code to predict whether the dump will fail to restore, because such code will never be as good as just trying the restore.
prior_attempts.reason: The author stopped responding after Noah Misch's March 2021 review, so the entry sat in Waiting on Author until Daniel Gustafsson returned it in November 2021. That review showed that the generated script still let the final pg_upgrade fail on a REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC, and that the check compared obj_ident without obj_type. Noah Misch also had doubts about the approach, since pg_upgrade code that predicts restore failures cannot match a real restore.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: [P14] predicted failing GRANT and REVOKE commands on changed catalog objects and wrote a fix script. This proposal predicts a duplicate FK name conflict and gives only a hint.

objections.title: Broad check makes --check fail for clusters that upgrade fine
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA's upgrade pipeline runs pg_upgrade --check as a gate. A cluster whose partition sorts before its parent, which would restore cleanly, now fails the gate. The DBA must rename production constraints before upgrading, or skip the check, to get past a failure that would never happen.
objections.argument: Message #5 reports 5 false positives against 5 real failures in 13 cases, so half of the reports block upgrades that work today. Today a --check failure means the upgrade will fail. The broad query turns some failures into advice, and the proposal still makes them fatal. The reviewer prefers the broad query so that a future pg_dump sort change cannot hide cases, but that trade costs users now for a risk that a test could catch. [P14] doubts that pg_upgrade code can predict restore failures as well as a real restore does.
objections.author_must_show: Why should cases that restore cleanly fail --check, instead of producing a warning or being excluded by the narrow query plus a test that pins pg_dump's sort order?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 confirms that v1 reports 5 cases that upgrade fine, and the check still fails for them. The reviewer accepted that cost, but no committer has, and the thread does not discuss a warning or a narrow query with a test.

objections.title: The check covers pg_upgrade only, but pg_dump ordering causes the failure
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs pg_dump on a 17 database with this layout and restores it into 18 with pg_restore. No check runs on that path, so the restore fails with the same "already exists" error. The user sees no hint.
objections.argument: Message #5 shows the restore works when the partition's own ADD CONSTRAINT comes before the ancestor's, because the clone then gets a generated name. A dump-order dependency in the new pg_dump could make that order hold for both pg_upgrade and plain dump/restore. Message #2 declines changes to pg_dump, but gives no technical reason. A committer would likely ask whether an ordering rule in pg_dump costs less than a permanent check that only helps one tool.
objections.author_must_show: Why is an ordering dependency in pg_dump, which would also fix plain dump/restore, worse than a check confined to pg_upgrade?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 declines a pg_dump change without a technical reason, and message #4 agrees on scope only. The plain-restore scenario is weaker than stated, since pg_restore continues after the error by default, but the design question stands.

objections.title: Master-only check misses most users who hit this upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A user upgrades from 17 to 18 or 19 with that release's pg_upgrade. --check still reports "Clusters are compatible" and the restore fails as in message #1. The new check never runs for them because it exists only in the PG20 pg_upgrade binary.
objections.argument: The check runs in the new cluster's pg_upgrade, and the affected source versions are 11 through 17. The thread targets master only (message #3), and the CommitFest entry is in the PG20 cycle. Users who upgrade from 17 to 18 or 19 in the next few years get no protection. A committer would likely ask whether a fix tagged Bugfix should be back-patched to the pg_upgrade of 18 and 19. The thread does not discuss this.
objections.author_must_show: Is the check intended for back-patch to the pg_upgrade of 18 and 19, and if not, how do users upgrading from 17 into those releases learn about this case?

critic.reasoning: The check runs in the new version's pg_upgrade, and message #3 targets master only. Upgrades from 17 into 18 or 19 keep the failure, and the thread does not discuss a back-patch.

objections.title: One report of an unusual schema; no wider demand shown
objections.failure_scenario: The check ships and runs on every pg_upgrade from 11-17 for years, but almost no cluster has a redundant NOT VALID FK on a partition with the parent's FK name. A user who does hit the case today gets a clear pg_restore error, renames the constraint, and reruns pg_upgrade with the old cluster intact.
objections.argument: The thread shows one reproducer from one reporter (message #1), with no field reports, -general or -bugs threads, or second user. Álvaro says the partition constraint has little use, and he is not convinced a check is worth it (message #2). The author agrees the fix is a drop or rename (message #3). The current failure happens before data transfer and names the constraint, so the cost of the workaround is one retry.
objections.author_must_show: How many users besides the original reporter have hit this restore failure, and did anyone find it hard to recover from?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows one reporter and one reproducer, and Álvaro in message #2 doubts the check is worth adding. The author's point that the error is not obvious does not show that the case is common.

refuted.title: Predictive restore check blocks upgrades that would succeed
refuted.failure_scenario: A user with parent zz_trn and partition aa_part, both with an FK named fk_trn_acc, runs pg_upgrade from 17. The restore would succeed, but the new check stops the upgrade. The user must rename a constraint to proceed, during an upgrade window.
refuted.argument: [P14] was not accepted partly because pg_upgrade code that predicts restore failures cannot match a real restore, and that reason holds here. Message #5 reports the v1 query flags 10 cases in its 13-case test, and only 5 of them fail. It also says a narrow query would copy pg_dump's sort order. The thread's answer is that false positives are rare and a rename fixes them, but Álvaro in message #2 was not convinced the check is worth adding at all.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is blocking about half of the flagged upgrades that would succeed better than a warning, or than a fix in pg_dump's ordering for 11-17 sources?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same false-positive problem and names the two alternatives more exactly.

refuted.title: Broad prediction check blocks upgrades that would succeed
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on 17 has a partition whose name sorts before its parent, with a same-named NOT VALID FK on both. Without the patch the upgrade works, but with it the --check run and the real run both stop at this check. The user must rename constraints before the upgrade can go ahead.
refuted.argument: Message #5 reports that v1 flags 5 cases that would have upgraded fine, the same count as the real failures it catches. The narrow query is rejected in message #5 because it would copy pg_dump's sort order, so either way pg_upgrade carries a model of restore behaviour that must track pg_dump. [P14] records the concern that pg_upgrade code that predicts restore failures will never be as good as running the restore. The check also has to stay as long as pg_upgrade accepts 11-17 old clusters.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is blocking about as many working upgrades as failing ones acceptable, compared with a fix that removes the failure?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The added maintenance point is weak, because the broad query does not depend on pg_dump's sort order and applies only to 11-17 old clusters.

refuted.title: The real pg_upgrade run already detects this, with fewer wrong answers
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on 15 has a partition that sorts before its parent, with a same-named NOT VALID FK. Today the upgrade succeeds. With the patch, --check fails before the maintenance window, and the user must rename a constraint that caused no problem.
refuted.argument: pg_upgrade restores the schema before it transfers any relation files, so a failed restore leaves the old cluster intact, and the error names the table and constraint. Message #5 shows the check flags 5 cases out of 13 where the real restore works, which the existing path never does. [P14] records a committer's view that pg_upgrade code which predicts restore failures "will never be as good as just trying the restore", and Álvaro in message #2 was not convinced either. The proposal's gain is earlier notice for a rare, redundant constraint that a rename fixes.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users hit this in the field, and why is earlier notice worth a permanent check that also blocks upgrades that would succeed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 and standards-compat-1. Its own point is weak: the real run needs the old server stopped, so it cannot give the advance notice that --check gives on a running cluster.

refuted.title: Per-pattern restore-failure checks do not pass the accumulation test
refuted.failure_scenario: Each rare schema that makes pg_restore fail gets its own query in check.c, with false positives and a version-gated TAP test. Over several releases maintainers carry many such checks for shrinking source-version ranges, and each one predicts the restore less well than running it.
refuted.argument: The same argument for this check fits any other restore failure caused by an odd but legal schema. The check also blocks 5 of 13 tested cases that would have upgraded fine (message #5), so some of the few affected users lose a working upgrade. The recorded reason in [P14] was that code predicting restore failures "will never be as good as just trying the restore", which applies here.
refuted.author_must_show: Why does this failure need a dedicated check when pg_upgrade already reports the exact constraint at restore time and the user can rename it and retry?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on future checks that the material does not show. check.c already holds many version-gated checks, this one costs only users with 11-17 old clusters, and the remaining demand point duplicates demand-1.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a new fatal check to pg_upgrade --check in src/bin/pg_upgrade/check.c.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: The failure comes from the order of pg_dump's ADD CONSTRAINT statements; the proposal leaves that order unchanged.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The entry is tagged Bugfix but targets master only, while affected upgrades from 17 go into 18 and 19.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The check and its version-gated TAP test stay as long as pg_upgrade accepts old clusters from 11 through 17.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The check predicts a restore failure that the real run already reports, an approach [P14] records doubts about.

questions: Why should cases that restore cleanly fail --check, instead of producing a warning or being excluded by a narrow query with a test that pins pg_dump's sort order?
Why is an ordering dependency in pg_dump, which would also fix plain dump and restore, worse than a check confined to pg_upgrade?
How many users besides the original reporter have hit this restore failure, and did anyone find it hard to recover from?
Is the check intended for back-patch to the pg_upgrade of 18 and 19, and if not, how do users upgrading from 17 learn about this case?
Does the author accept the v2-0002 changes to the report and the hint?

committability.owner_note: Álvaro Herrera replied in message #2 but was not convinced, and has not replied to the patch or to v2. The owner needs to know pg_upgrade checks and partition FK handling.
committability.liability: A fatal pg_upgrade check with known false positives, kept while old clusters from 11 through 17 are supported, plus a TAP test that runs only with an old install.
committability.author_follow_up: The author returned after six weeks with a patch and offered to add a test, but has not replied to v2.

priority.reason: The patch touches one file and affects only clusters with a same-named NOT VALID FK on a partition and its parent. The thread must first settle whether cases that would upgrade fine should fail the check.

provisional_note: Without the code, the query's handling of multi-level partition hierarchies and of the 11-16 catalogs could not be judged. The false-positive counts come from the reviewer's report in message #5 only.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade: Support for upgrading to checksums enabled
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets pg_upgrade run between clusters with different data checksum settings by rewriting page checksums while it copies files. The first version did this automatically in --copy mode, and a later version added an explicit --update-checksums option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author closed the entry because reviewers showed little interest in the feature or in solving its remaining problems. One problem was still open: copyFile() has a separate Windows code path, and the author did not know how checksum rewriting should work there. He said the feature could not move ahead without an answer to it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reducing memory usage of creating foreign key between partitioned tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes RelationBuildPartitionDesc build a partitioned table's partition descriptor in a temporary memory context and delete that context afterwards, so the temporary memory is freed instead of being leaked. The aim was to stop the out-of-memory failures seen when adding a foreign key between two partitioned tables that each have thousands of partitions; later revisions were discussed for back-patching to v12.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected early that leak management belongs at the caller level, not inside RelationBuildPartitionDesc. Amit Langote then noted that commit 5b9312378 had already removed the repeated rebuild that caused the leak in v13, so the remaining question was back-patching. Tom Lane found no visible leak in HEAD and saw that the test case was still impractical because of planner cost in RI_Initial_Check, so he saw no reason to back-patch a leak fix. He recommended rejecting the patch and suggested back-porting 5b9312378 instead if a back-branch fix were wanted.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade version and path checking
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set makes pg_upgrade check every executable it uses, require the new binaries to match pg_upgrade's exact major and minor version, and default --new-bindir to pg_upgrade's own directory. It came from Tom Lane's report that pg_upgrade 11.3 would use pg_dump 11.1.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut committed 0002 to 0004, which add the executable checks, the --new-bindir default and a typo fix. He found that 0001 compares pg_upgrade's version only with pg_ctl's, so it does not make all binaries match, and proposed a version check for each validate_exec() call instead. On 2019-09-02 the author said a new version would come that week, but no later version appears in the visible messages.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It compares (new_cluster.bin_version != PG_VERSION_NUM), but new_cluster.bin_version is actually just the version of pg_ctl, so this is just comparing the version of pg_upgrade with the version of pg_ctl, which is not wrong, but doesn't really achieve the full goal of having all binaries match.

precedents_retrieved.title: avoid bitmapOR-ing indexes for scan conditions implied by partition constraint
precedents_retrieved.authors: Justin Pryzby (justinpryzby), Soumyadeep Chakraborty (soumyadeep2007), Soumyadeep Chakraborty (soumyadeepc)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner skip bitmap index scans for arms of an OR clause that the partition constraint refutes, so each partition scans only the useful arms. The change lives in generate_bitmap_or_paths() in indxpath.c and targets queries with long OR lists over many partitions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to fixing this in indxpath.c. The fix helps only bitmap scans, may repeat the same proof, cannot be turned off, leaves row estimates unchanged, and may break the loop that requires each OR arm to match an index. He proposed removing proven quals from baserestrictinfo instead, but measured about 2.5% slowdown on pgbench -S and left the direction open. The entry then sat in Waiting on Author for weeks, and Masahiko Sawada returned it with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade data type check connection overhead reduction
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the pg_upgrade data type checks from separate functions, each looping over all databases, into a struct that one umbrella check uses. All data type queries then run against a database over a single connection, which cuts connectToServer overhead in the --check phase.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No design objection was raised, and the reviewer called the patch in decent shape. After v10 the patch stopped applying to master, and the author posted no rebase after the CF manager asked for one. The entry was returned with feedback for that reason.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade check for Unicode update
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Joe Conway, Nathan Bossart
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a pg_upgrade check that detects a change in the Unicode version between the old and new clusters. When the version changes, pg_upgrade warns and writes a list of relations that may be affected, such as indexes using the builtin provider, to a file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No message states the withdrawal, but the last messages show reviewers favoring another approach. Robert Haas and Joe Conway argued that stability needs support for old Unicode versions alongside new ones, and Jeff Davis answered with a plan for versioned collation and ctype providers. Nathan Bossart asked whether a warning is enough and what users should do with the list of relations.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The way to actually provide the stability that people want here is to continue supporting old versions while adding support for new versions.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_upgrade documentation improvement
precedents_retrieved.summary: A documentation patch for pg_upgrade explained what "compatible initdb flags" means for the new cluster: the same encoding, locale and checksum settings as the old one. It told users to find the encoding and locale of template0 with psql -l and the checksum setting with pg_controldata.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut said the cluster locale is better taken from pg_controldata and doubted that pg_upgrade needs the encoding to match. The author asked whether to change the patch to use pg_controldata only, but no revised patch followed. Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback because the thread had died.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 8355a011a0124bdf7ccbada206a967d427039553, which
turns out to have been a misguided effort.  We can't really support
this in a partitioning hierarchy after all for exactly the reasons
stated in the documentation removed by that commit.  It's still
possible to use ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING (or for that matter ON
CONFLICT .. DO UPDATE) on individual partitions if desired, but
but to allow this on a partitioned table implies that we have some
way of evaluating uniqueness across the whole partitioning
hierarchy, which is false.

Shinoda Noriyoshi noticed that the old code was crashing (which we
could fix, though not in a nice way) and Amit Langote realized
that this was indicative of a fundamental problem with the commit
being reverted here.

roaster_notes.note: [P8] is about Unicode version changes, and its recorded reason does not apply here.
The proposal leaves pg_dump output, SQL syntax, GUCs and psql unchanged. The two objections concern the --check contract and the release scope.

The patch adds a read-only catalog query to pg_upgrade --check on the old cluster. It does not change on-disk format, WAL, the catalogs, the wire protocol or any extension-facing API, and pg_dump output stays the same. Whether a restore-predicting check is worth its false positives ([P14]) is a design question for other angles.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. The new check is a read-only catalog query that pg_upgrade already runs as the install user against the old cluster. It adds no SQL surface, role, GUC or default, and v2 quotes the reported names. Not checked without the code: whether the report file is written with the same permissions as other pg_upgrade report files.
Hot-path cost is not a concern here, because the check runs only during pg_upgrade against 11-17 old clusters.
One objection only. The material names no extension or other core feature that already detects this conflict.
Demand is the weak point: one reporter, and a committer who doubts the check is worth adding.
